question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Compare a traditional Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document with an Agile Product Backlog. Specifically, compare them in terms of when the requirements are fully detailed and how the documents handle changes requested by the client.
rubric: 2 marks for comparing detail timing (SRS upfront vs. Backlog incremental/just-in-time). 2 marks for comparing change management (SRS formal control vs. Backlog continuous reprioritization).
model_answer: In an SRS, all requirements are thoroughly detailed, formatted, and formalized entirely upfront before any development begins. Changes to an SRS require a formal, heavy change-control approval process. In contrast, an Agile Product Backlog details requirements incrementally—only the items at the top are detailed just before a sprint, while items at the bottom remain vague. Changes are handled flexibly through continuous reprioritization by the Product Owner without needing formal document revisions.

question_text: A core mechanism of the Kanban method is the enforcement of Work-In-Progress (WIP) limits. Explain exactly what a WIP limit is on a Kanban board, and describe two ways this constraint improves a development team's overall throughput and efficiency.
rubric: 1 mark for defining WIP limits as column caps. 2 mark for the benefit of reducing context switching/focusing on finishing. 1 mark for the benefit of exposing bottlenecks.
model_answer: A WIP limit is a strict maximum number of task cards allowed in a specific column of the Kanban board at any given time. This improves efficiency by (1) forcing teams to stop starting new tasks and focus on finishing current ones (reducing context switching), and (2) immediately making system bottlenecks visually obvious so the whole team can swarm to resolve the blockage.

question_text: According to the IEEE definition, software consists of three essential components. Identify these three components and explain why treating a software project simply as "writing lines of code" can lead to severe maintainability issues later in the product's lifecycle.

model_answer: Backward traceability links a requirement back to its original business goal or stakeholder, explaining why it exists. Forward traceability links a requirement forward to the specific system designs, code modules, and test cases that implement it. question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. Software failures can happen in every phase in software development and maintenance unlike the hardware.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: A core mechanism of the Kanban method is the enforcement of Work-In-Progress (WIP) limits. Explain exactly what a WIP limit is on a Kanban board, and describe two ways this constraint improves a development team's overall throughput and efficiency.

model_answer: A WIP limit is a strict maximum number of task cards allowed in a specific column of the Kanban board at any given time. question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. model_answer: In an SRS, all requirements are thoroughly detailed, formatted, and formalized entirely upfront before any development begins. Changes to an SRS require a formal, heavy change-control approval process. In contrast, an Agile Product Backlog details requirements incrementally—only the items at the top are detailed just before a sprint, while items at the bottom remain vague. Changes are handled flexibly through continuous reprioritization by the Product Owner without needing formal document revisions.

question_text: A core mechanism of the Kanban method is the enforcement of Work-In-Progress (WIP) limits. Explain exactly what a WIP limit is on a Kanban board, and describe two ways this constraint improves a development team's overall throughput and efficiency.
rubric: 1 mark for defining WIP limits as column caps. 2 mark for the benefit of reducing context switching/focusing on finishing. 1 mark for the benefit of exposing bottlenecks.
model_answer: A WIP limit is a strict maximum number of task cards allowed in a specific column of the Kanban board at any given time. question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Requirements traceability is a crucial part of managing scope in large projects. Define both forward and backward traceability and explain a specific scenario where forward traceability is essential when a client requests a sudden modification to a requirement.
rubric: 1 mark for defining backward traceability. 1 mark for defining forward traceability. 2 mark for explaining the necessity of forward traceability for impact analysis during modifications.
model_answer: Backward traceability links a requirement back to its original business goal or stakeholder, explaining why it exists. Forward traceability links a requirement forward to the specific system designs, code modules, and test cases that implement it. If a client requests a sudden modification, forward traceability is essential because it allows the team to perform an impact analysis—instantly identifying exactly which lines of code and which test cases need to be rewritten to accommodate the change.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. question_text: Requirements traceability is a crucial part of managing scope in large projects. Define both forward and backward traceability and explain a specific scenario where forward traceability is essential when a client requests a sudden modification to a requirement.

model_answer: Backward traceability links a requirement back to its original business goal or stakeholder, explaining why it exists. question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.
student_answer: Hardware : manufactured physical components. often follows a bathtub failure curve: early failures , stable useful life ,wear out.  software: does not physically wear out. failures arise from defects/incorrect assumptions. changes may introduce new faults, producing failure spikes and logical deterioration. Refactoring, regression testing and clean architecture reduce deterioration.

question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

Green - This includes writing the minimum code needed to pass a test.      Refactor - This is the clean up process. Following this disciple benefits to get rapid defect feedback, regress safely, define executable specifications and pressure toward simple/testable designs.

model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. model_answer: A WIP limit is a strict maximum number of task cards allowed in a specific column of the Kanban board at any given time. This improves efficiency by (1) forcing teams to stop starting new tasks and focus on finishing current ones (reducing context switching), and (2) immediately making system bottlenecks visually obvious so the whole team can swarm to resolve the blockage.
student_answer: The Work-In-Progress is the maximum number of work items allowed in a workflow stage at any given time.   1. This also allows to focus completely on the work started in that working stage. question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

question_text: According to the IEEE definition, software consists of three essential components. Identify these three components and explain why treating a software project simply as "writing lines of code" can lead to severe maintainability issues later in the product's lifecycle.
rubric: 2 mark for listing all three components correctly. 1 mark for explaining the role of documentation in future understanding. 1 mark for linking the lack of non-code components directly to increased maintenance costs or errors.
model_answer: The three components are (1) Instructions (programs/code), (2) Data Structures, and (3) Documentation. Treating software merely as code ignores the importance of data structures and documentation. Without clear documentation and organized data models, future developers will struggle to understand the system's logic, making bug fixes and feature updates (maintenance) significantly slower, more expensive, and highly prone to causing new errors.

question_text: Requirements traceability is a crucial part of managing scope in large projects. Define both forward and backward traceability and explain a specific scenario where forward traceability is essential when a client requests a sudden modification to a requirement.
rubric: 1 mark for defining backward traceability. 1 mark for defining forward traceability. 2 mark for explaining the necessity of forward traceability for impact analysis during modifications.
model_answer: Backward traceability links a requirement back to its original business goal or stakeholder, explaining why it exists. Forward traceability links a requirement forward to the specific system designs, code modules, and test cases that implement it. If a client requests a sudden modification, forward traceability is essential because it allows the team to perform an impact analysis—instantly identifying exactly which lines of code and which test cases need to be rewritten to accommodate the change.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Explain why the non-functional requirement "The system shall load pages quickly and be highly reliable" is considered a poorly written, critical failure in software engineering. Then rewrite it as two separate statements each with precise, measurable metrics that a QA engineer could test.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining the subjective/untestable nature of the original. 2 mark for a rewritten, measurable performance metric. 1 mark for a rewritten, measurable reliability metric.
model_answer: The requirement is a failure because terms like "quickly" and "highly reliable" are ambiguous, subjective, and completely untestable by QA engineers, as different people interpret them differently. Rewritten: (1) "The system shall load the user dashboard in under 2.0 seconds for 95% of all requests." (2) "The system shall maintain 99.9% uptime during a calendar month."

question_text: Compare a traditional Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document with an Agile Product Backlog. Specifically, compare them in terms of when the requirements are fully detailed and how the documents handle changes requested by the client.
rubric: 2 marks for comparing detail timing (SRS upfront vs. Backlog incremental/just-in-time). 2 marks for comparing change management (SRS formal control vs. Backlog continuous reprioritization).
model_answer: In an SRS, all requirements are thoroughly detailed, formatted, and formalized entirely upfront before any development begins. Changes to an SRS require a formal, heavy change-control approval process. In contrast, an Agile Product Backlog details requirements incrementally—only the items at the top are detailed just before a sprint, while items at the bottom remain vague. Changes are handled flexibly through continuous reprioritization by the Product Owner without needing formal document revisions.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. question_text: A core mechanism of the Kanban method is the enforcement of Work-In-Progress (WIP) limits. Explain exactly what a WIP limit is on a Kanban board, and describe two ways this constraint improves a development team's overall throughput and efficiency.
rubric: 1 mark for defining WIP limits as column caps. 2 mark for the benefit of reducing context switching/focusing on finishing. 1 mark for the benefit of exposing bottlenecks.
model_answer: A WIP limit is a strict maximum number of task cards allowed in a specific column of the Kanban board at any given time. This improves efficiency by (1) forcing teams to stop starting new tasks and focus on finishing current ones (reducing context switching), and (2) immediately making system bottlenecks visually obvious so the whole team can swarm to resolve the blockage.

student_answer: Adaptive maintenance: This is done to make sure the system can efficiently be adapted to new hardware, OS updates, change in regulations or newly emerging APIs.   Preventive maintenance: This is done before failures occur by anticipating them to ensure the system is reliable and maintainable in-case of such an occurrence.      Consider a library management system.   Adaptive maintenance: After a period of using the system with borrowers using a scanable card with as identification, it is decided to be replaced with a fingerprint system for convenience. model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: A core mechanism of the Kanban method is the enforcement of Work-In-Progress (WIP) limits. Explain exactly what a WIP limit is on a Kanban board, and describe two ways this constraint improves a development team's overall throughput and efficiency.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. model_answer: Two types of waste are "Partially done work" (code sitting in a branch not deployed) and "Extra features" (building things the customer didn't ask for). model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

question_text: The Rapid Application Development (RAD) model heavily utilizes parallel teams and component reuse to achieve 60-90 day timeboxes. Explain how this approach accelerates development time and identify one major project risk if the system's architecture cannot be easily modularized.
rubric: 2 marks for explaining the acceleration mechanism (parallel work and reuse). 2 mark for explaining that lack of modularity breaks parallel integration and causes the project to fail.
model_answer: RAD accelerates development by having multiple teams work simultaneously on different functional components of the system while heavily reusing existing, pre-tested code rather than writing from scratch. If the system architecture cannot be easily modularized, the parallel teams will be blocked by dependencies, unable to integrate their work, and the strict 60-90 day timebox will inevitably fail.

question_text: Verification and Validation are two concepts that are often confused, but they actually answer very different questions about software quality. rubric: 1 mark for Verification definition/question and 1 mark for its technique. 1 mark for Validation definition/question and 1 mark for its technique.

question_text: Requirements traceability is a crucial part of managing scope in large projects. Define both forward and backward traceability and explain a specific scenario where forward traceability is essential when a client requests a sudden modification to a requirement.
rubric: 1 mark for defining backward traceability. 1 mark for defining forward traceability. 2 mark for explaining the necessity of forward traceability for impact analysis during modifications.
model_answer: Backward traceability links a requirement back to its original business goal or stakeholder, explaining why it exists. Forward traceability links a requirement forward to the specific system designs, code modules, and test cases that implement it. question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.
student_answer: Bath tub curve shows high early failure rate, rising again at end of life, low during useful life.

question_text: Compare a traditional Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document with an Agile Product Backlog. Specifically, compare them in terms of when the requirements are fully detailed and how the documents handle changes requested by the client.

model_answer: In an SRS, all requirements are thoroughly detailed, formatted, and formalized entirely upfront before any development begins. Changes are handled flexibly through continuous reprioritization by the Product Owner without needing formal document revisions.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

model_answer: A WIP limit is a strict maximum number of task cards allowed in a specific column of the Kanban board at any given time. question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? model_answer: Relying solely on interviews is limited because stakeholders often struggle to articulate their actual needs, they frequently describe imagined solutions rather than underlying problems, and they routinely forget to mention "obvious" daily tasks. Direct observation provides unique insights by revealing tacit knowledge showing the engineer what users actually do in their real environment, including workarounds and undocumented processes that they would never mention in an interview room.
student_answer: Relying solely on interviews to gather requirements is challenging because, most of the time stakeholders cant articulate their needs and different stakeholders might have different conflicting requirements. Also requirements are keep changing as the stakeholders change their minds.   Direct observation helps identify implicit requirements and unstated assumptions which cannot gather by conducting a conversation. Also it helps to identify needs that are needed by the stakeholder in a completely different perspective.

question_text: According to the IEEE definition, software consists of three essential components. Identify these three components and explain why treating a software project simply as "writing lines of code" can lead to severe maintainability issues later in the product's lifecycle.
rubric: 2 mark for listing all three components correctly. 1 mark for explaining the role of documentation in future understanding. 1 mark for linking the lack of non-code components directly to increased maintenance costs or errors.
model_answer: The three components are (1) Instructions (programs/code), (2) Data Structures, and (3) Documentation. Treating software merely as code ignores the importance of data structures and documentation. Without clear documentation and organized data models, future developers will struggle to understand the system's logic, making bug fixes and feature updates (maintenance) significantly slower, more expensive, and highly prone to causing new errors.
student_answer: 1.instructions   2.associated data   3.documentation

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.
student_answer: Hardware  is manufactured from physical components and those components wear-out overtime. Hardware failure shows a bathtub curve because its failure rates are early in the lifetime and then stabled during useful life but finally they wear out. But when it comes to software they do not physically wear out; failures in software arise from defects or incorrect assumptions. When changes introduce new faults in software, the curve produce a spike pattern in software failure curve.

question_text: Compare a traditional Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document with an Agile Product Backlog. Specifically, compare them in terms of when the requirements are fully detailed and how the documents handle changes requested by the client.
rubric: 2 marks for comparing detail timing (SRS upfront vs. Backlog incremental/just-in-time). 2 marks for comparing change management (SRS formal control vs. Backlog continuous reprioritization).
model_answer: In an SRS, all requirements are thoroughly detailed, formatted, and formalized entirely upfront before any development begins. Changes to an SRS require a formal, heavy change-control approval process. In contrast, an Agile Product Backlog details requirements incrementally—only the items at the top are detailed just before a sprint, while items at the bottom remain vague. Changes are handled flexibly through continuous reprioritization by the Product Owner without needing formal document revisions.
student_answer: SRS is a complete description of the software system to be built. Product backlog is an ordered, ever evolving list and it is never finished. When the requirements are fully detailed SRS becomes clear and complete while in product backlog it is listed from top to bottom, top as the ready to bult and bottom as the vague requirements.

question_text: The Rapid Application Development (RAD) model heavily utilizes parallel teams and component reuse to achieve 60-90 day timeboxes. Explain how this approach accelerates development time and identify one major project risk if the system's architecture cannot be easily modularized.
rubric: 2 marks for explaining the acceleration mechanism (parallel work and reuse). 2 mark for explaining that lack of modularity breaks parallel integration and causes the project to fail.
model_answer: RAD accelerates development by having multiple teams work simultaneously on different functional components of the system while heavily reusing existing, pre-tested code rather than writing from scratch. If the system architecture cannot be easily modularized, the parallel teams will be blocked by dependencies, unable to integrate their work, and the strict 60-90 day timebox will inevitably fail.

question_text: Lean software development focuses primarily on the principle of "Eliminating Waste." Identify two specific types of waste in a software engineering context and explain how a development team might change their process to eliminate them.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the first waste type and 1 mark for a valid elimination strategy. 1 mark for identifying the second waste type and 1 mark for a valid elimination strategy.
model_answer: Two types of waste are "Partially done work" (code sitting in a branch not deployed) and "Extra features" (building things the customer didn't ask for). To eliminate partially done work, a team could implement Continuous Integration (CI) to merge code daily. To eliminate extra features, a team could use Throwaway Prototyping to validate customer needs before committing resources to full development.

question_text: The Waterfall model relies heavily on comprehensive, straightforward documentation. Discuss two major limitations of this sequential approach when dealing with complex, modern software systems where stakeholders are unsure of what they need at the start of the project.
rubric: 2 marks for explaining the limitation regarding the inability to freeze requirements upfront. 2 marks for explaining the limitation of late visibility/testing leading to expensive rework.
model_answer: First, Waterfall assumes requirements can be perfectly defined upfront, which is rarely true; stakeholders often change their minds as business needs shift, making early documents quickly obsolete. Second, the customer does not see a working version of the software until very late in the cycle (during integration/system testing). If the initial requirements were misunderstood, discovering this at the end results in catastrophic rework costs.
student_answer: When working with a waterfall mode, the customer only sees working software after many of the steps are already completed. This is time consuming and the delivery of the products are relatively late compared to other faster models. As a result this model is not suitable for projects that require the deliverables fast.      Requirement changes are costly when working with a waterfall model. The need for requirement changes can only be properly identified after feedback, and it arrives only in the later stages of the model. This requires all steps of the process, including requirement redefinition, redesign and implementation, testing and operation, to be rerun at great cost before the changes can be addressed.

question_text: Software requirements can be classified into functional, non-functional, and domain specific categories. Give a comprehensive definition of what a domain specific requirement is and use a brief example to explain how a domain requirement can lead to the creation of a non-functional requirement.
rubric: 2 mark for defining Domain requirements as external/legal constraints. 2 marks for a logical example showing a domain rule triggering a specific non-functional quality attribute.
model_answer: A Domain requirement is a constraint that originates from the operating environment, industry standards, or legal regulations, explaining WHY certain rules exist. For example, a healthcare law (Domain requirement) might dictate that patient data must be kept completely confidential. This directly forces the creation of a Non-Functional security requirement, such as "The system must encrypt all patient databases using AES-256 standards."
student_answer: Domain requirements are requirements that arise in order to be compliant with laws and regulations, and industry or operating environment conditions. These are often non-negotiable requirements. These requirements address "why" a particular systems is designed and deployed in a certain manner.      For example, in a medicine dispensing system, all medical records and activity needs to be stored which is a domain requirement. This leads to a non functional requirement of the system to be able to securely accommodate 100% of the required data.

question_text: Requirements traceability is a crucial part of managing scope in large projects. Define both forward and backward traceability and explain a specific scenario where forward traceability is essential when a client requests a sudden modification to a requirement.
rubric: 1 mark for defining backward traceability. 1 mark for defining forward traceability. 2 mark for explaining the necessity of forward traceability for impact analysis during modifications.
model_answer: Backward traceability links a requirement back to its original business goal or stakeholder, explaining why it exists. Forward traceability links a requirement forward to the specific system designs, code modules, and test cases that implement it. If a client requests a sudden modification, forward traceability is essential because it allows the team to perform an impact analysis—instantly identifying exactly which lines of code and which test cases need to be rewritten to accommodate the change.
student_answer: Backward traceability is the ability to trace a requirement back to a stakeholder need or a specific goal that specific requirement originated from. In short, tracing the cause based on the effects.   Forward traceability if the ability to trace the design, code and the tests that stemmed from a specific requirement. In short, tracing the effects based on the cause.      When a requirement modification is requested forward traceability becomes useful in finding the current implementation status, and the solutions designed to address that particular requirement. This provides a better understanding of what needs to be changed and how, with the context of the work already done, to respond to the requirement change appropriately.

question_text: The Agile Manifesto explicitly states that teams should value "Responding to change over following a plan." Explain what this principle means in practice for a development team's daily workflow and why it provides a strategic advantage in highly competitive markets.
rubric: 2 marks for explaining how it affects workflow (flexible short-term planning, reprioritizing backlogs). 2 mark for explaining the strategic/competitive advantage of adaptability.
model_answer: In practice, this means the team does not rigidly adhere to a year-long project schedule if new information arises. Instead, they keep their plans short-term and flexible, frequently reprioritizing their backlog based on new feedback. This provides a strategic advantage because it allows the business to adapt immediately to competitor moves or changing customer preferences, delivering relevant value rather than obsolete features.

question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Extreme Programming (XP) requires teams to practice Test Driven Development (TDD). Describe the three sequential steps in the TDD "Red-Green Refactor" cycle, and explain how following this discipline affects the long term cost of maintaining software.
rubric: 1 mark for Red description. 1 mark for Green description. 1 mark for Refactor description. 1 mark for linking TDD to early defect detection and reduced maintenance costs.
model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

model_answer: In an SRS, all requirements are thoroughly detailed, formatted, and formalized entirely upfront before any development begins. model_answer: First (Red), the developer writes a failing automated test for a new feature. Second (Green), they write the minimum amount of production code required to make that test pass. Third (Refactor), they clean up and optimize the code structure while ensuring the test still passes. Practicing TDD drastically reduces long term maintenance costs because defects are caught immediately during development when they are cheapest to fix, rather than later in production.

Forward traceability links a requirement forward to the specific system designs, code modules, and test cases that implement it. If a client requests a sudden modification, forward traceability is essential because it allows the team to perform an impact analysis—instantly identifying exactly which lines of code and which test cases need to be rewritten to accommodate the change.

question_text: Software maintenance accounts for roughly 60-80% of total lifecycle costs. Describe two specific types of software maintenance activities that contribute to this high cost and providing a practical example of why a team would perform each.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the first maintenance type and 1 mark for its valid example. 1 mark for identifying the second maintenance type and 1 mark for its valid example.
model_answer: Two types are Adaptive Maintenance and Perfective Maintenance (Corrective or Preventive are also valid). Adaptive maintenance involves modifying the system to cope with a changing environment, for example, updating an application because Apple released a new iOS version. Perfective maintenance involves improving performance or adding new features based on user feedback, such as adding a new report export feature to a portal.

question_text: The Rapid Application Development (RAD) model heavily utilizes parallel teams and component reuse to achieve 60-90 day timeboxes. Explain how this approach accelerates development time and identify one major project risk if the system's architecture cannot be easily modularized.
rubric: 2 marks for explaining the acceleration mechanism (parallel work and reuse). 2 mark for explaining that lack of modularity breaks parallel integration and causes the project to fail.
model_answer: RAD accelerates development by having multiple teams work simultaneously on different functional components of the system while heavily reusing existing, pre-tested code rather than writing from scratch. If the system architecture cannot be easily modularized, the parallel teams will be blocked by dependencies, unable to integrate their work, and the strict 60-90 day timebox will inevitably fail.

question_text: Explain why the non-functional requirement "The system shall load pages quickly and be highly reliable" is considered a poorly written, critical failure in software engineering. Then rewrite it as two separate statements each with precise, measurable metrics that a QA engineer could test.
rubric: 1 mark for explaining the subjective/untestable nature of the original. 2 mark for a rewritten, measurable performance metric. 1 mark for a rewritten, measurable reliability metric.
model_answer: The requirement is a failure because terms like "quickly" and "highly reliable" are ambiguous, subjective, and completely untestable by QA engineers, as different people interpret them differently. Rewritten: (1) "The system shall load the user dashboard in under 2.0 seconds for 95% of all requests." (2) "The system shall maintain 99.9% uptime during a calendar month."

question_text: Lean software development focuses primarily on the principle of "Eliminating Waste." Identify two specific types of waste in a software engineering context and explain how a development team might change their process to eliminate them.
rubric: 1 mark for identifying the first waste type and 1 mark for a valid elimination strategy. 1 mark for identifying the second waste type and 1 mark for a valid elimination strategy.
model_answer: Two types of waste are "Partially done work" (code sitting in a branch not deployed) and "Extra features" (building things the customer didn't ask for). To eliminate partially done work, a team could implement Continuous Integration (CI) to merge code daily. To eliminate extra features, a team could use Throwaway Prototyping to validate customer needs before committing resources to full development.

question_text: According to the IEEE definition, software consists of three essential components. Identify these three components and explain why treating a software project simply as "writing lines of code" can lead to severe maintainability issues later in the product's lifecycle.
rubric: 2 mark for listing all three components correctly. 1 mark for explaining the role of documentation in future understanding. 1 mark for linking the lack of non-code components directly to increased maintenance costs or errors.
model_answer: The three components are (1) Instructions (programs/code), (2) Data Structures, and (3) Documentation. Treating software merely as code ignores the importance of data structures and documentation. Without clear documentation and organized data models, future developers will struggle to understand the system's logic, making bug fixes and feature updates (maintenance) significantly slower, more expensive, and highly prone to causing new errors.

question_text: Hardware reliability is often described using the classic "bathtub curve". How does this compare to what we actually see with software failure rates over time? In particular, why does software tend to show a repeated "spike" pattern throughout its operational life, instead of following the same curve as hardware?
rubric: 1 mark for describing the hardware bathtub curve/wear and tear. 1 mark for stating software does not physically wear out. 2 mark for explaining that the spikes are caused by side effects introduced during code changes.
model_answer: Hardware follows a bathtub curve where failures are high early on (manufacturing defects), drop to a stable low, and then rise at the end due to physical wear and tear. Software does not physically wear out. However, its failure rate exhibits a spike pattern because every time a developer introduces a change, new feature, or bug fix, there is a high risk of introducing new logical defects (side effects) that cause the failure rate to spike temporarily until patched.

question_text: Verification and Validation are two concepts that are often confused, but they actually answer very different questions about software quality. Define both terms, including the core question each one is trying to answer and give one example of a testing or inspection technique commonly used for each.
rubric: 1 mark for Verification definition/question and 1 mark for its technique. 1 mark for Validation definition/question and 1 mark for its technique.
model_answer: Verification asks, "Are we building the product right?" It checks if the software internally conforms to its written design specifications. A technique for this is a formal code review or static analysis. Validation asks, "Are we building the right product?" It checks if the software meets the real-world needs of the end users. A technique for this is User Acceptance Testing (UAT) or prototype evaluation with customers.

question_text: The Waterfall model relies heavily on comprehensive, straightforward documentation. Discuss two major limitations of this sequential approach when dealing with complex, modern software systems where stakeholders are unsure of what they need at the start of the project.
rubric: 2 marks for explaining the limitation regarding the inability to freeze requirements upfront. 2 marks for explaining the limitation of late visibility/testing leading to expensive rework.
model_answer: First, Waterfall assumes requirements can be perfectly defined upfront, which is rarely true; stakeholders often change their minds as business needs shift, making early documents quickly obsolete. Second, the customer does not see a working version of the software until very late in the cycle (during integration/system testing). If the initial requirements were misunderstood, discovering this at the end results in catastrophic rework costs.
